title: Die drei grünen Zweige
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 206. Text from Wikisource („Die drei grünen Zweige (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: An old hermit who has spent years carrying water up a mountainside each evening, guided by an angel, condemns a criminal being led to the gallows with a careless word of judgment — and loses the angel's company for it. Told by a bird that only God may judge, he carries a dry branch as penance, sleeping on it and begging his bread door to door, until three green twigs are found grown from the wood beneath his head on the morning he is found dead, after a night in which his story moved three robbers to repent.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein Einsiedler, der lebte in einem Walde an dem Fuße eines Berges und brachte seine Zeit in Gebet und guten Werken zu,
sentences.l: There was once a hermit, who lived in a forest at the foot of a mountain and spent his time in prayer and good works,
sentences.i: There was once a hermit who lived in a forest at the foot of a mountain, and passed his time in prayer and good works,
sentences.n: “Einsiedler” is one who lives apart — a hermit. “brachte … zu” is the separable verb “zubringen,” to spend (time); the particle “zu” sits at the far end of the clause, as separable prefixes do in a main-clause past. “Werken” is the dative plural of “das Werk” — deeds, works, in the religious sense of the tale.

sentences.t: und jeden Abend trug er noch zur Ehre Gottes ein paar Eimer Wasser den Berg hinauf.
sentences.l: and every evening he still carried, to the honor of God, a couple of pails of water up the mountain.
sentences.i: and every evening he would still carry a few pails of water up the mountain in honor of God.
sentences.n: “jeden Abend” is the accusative of time — every evening. “noch” here is ‘on top of that, in addition’ — the water-carrying is beyond his other devotions. “den Berg hinauf” is the accusative of extent — up the length of the mountain.

sentences.t: Manches Thier wurde damit getränkt und manche Pflanze damit erquickt,
sentences.l: Many an animal was given drink with it and many a plant refreshed with it,
sentences.i: Many an animal was watered by it, and many a plant refreshed,
sentences.n: “Thier” is the 1857 spelling of “Tier.” “getränkt” is the past participle of “tränken,” to give (an animal) to drink; “Pflanze” is “die Pflanze,” plant. The parallelism (“manches … manche …”) is the tale's plain formula for ‘all sorts.’

sentences.t: denn auf den Anhöhen weht beständig ein harter Wind, der die Luft und die Erde austrocknet,
sentences.l: for on the heights there constantly blows a harsh wind, which dries out the air and the earth,
sentences.i: for on the heights a hard wind blows constantly, drying out both the air and the earth,
sentences.n: “die Anhöhen” is the plural of “die Anhöhe,” a rise, a height (an- + Höhe). “harter Wind” — the wind is “hard,” not merely strong: an old, plain adjective for weather that punishes.

sentences.t: und die wilden Vögel, die vor den Menschen scheuen, kreißen dann hoch und suchen mit ihren scharfen Augen nach einem Trunk.
sentences.l: and the wild birds, which shy from people, circle then high and search with their sharp eyes for a drink.
sentences.i: and the wild birds, which shy from people, wheel high in the air and search with their sharp eyes for a draught.
sentences.n: “scheuen vor” + dative = to shy away from. “kreißen” is an older verb for circling in flight, wheeling (a variant beside “kreisen”); the modern reader who knows only “kreißen” for a woman in labor should not be misled — the older sense of turning in a circle is what the text has here.

sentences.t: Und weil der Einsiedler so fromm war, so gieng ein Engel Gottes, seinen Augen sichtbar, mit ihm hinauf, zählte seine Schritte und brachte ihm, wenn die Arbeit vollendet war, sein Essen,
sentences.l: And because the hermit was so devout, so an angel of God, visible to his eyes, went up with him, counted his steps and brought him, when the work was finished, his food,
sentences.i: And because the hermit was so devout, an angel of God, visible to his eyes, went up with him, counted his steps, and brought him his food when the work was done,
sentences.n: The second “so” is the resumptive “so” that a German main clause takes after an initial subordinate clause (weil … so gieng …); a natural English rendering drops it. “seinen Augen sichtbar” is a dative absolute — “visible to his eyes,” the whole point being that the angel is not merely present but seen. “gieng” is the 1857 spelling of “ging.”

sentences.t: so wie jener Prophet auf Gottes Geheiß von den Raben gespeiset ward.
sentences.l: just as that prophet on God's bidding was fed by the ravens.
sentences.i: just as that prophet, at God's bidding, was fed by the ravens.
sentences.n: A reference to Elijah in 1 Kings 17, fed by ravens in the wilderness — the tale takes the biblical episode for granted. “gespeiset” is a slightly older form of “gespeist,” the past participle of “speisen,” to feed, to give a meal to; “ward” is the archaic past of “werden,” now “wurde.”

sentences.t: Als der Einsiedler in seiner Frömmigkeit schon zu einem hohen Alter gekommen war, da trug es sich zu, daß er einmal von weitem sah wie man einen armen Sünder zum Galgen führte.
sentences.l: When the hermit had already, in his piety, come to a great age, it came to pass that he once saw from a distance how a poor sinner was being led to the gallows.
sentences.i: When the hermit had already come to a great age in his piety, it came to pass that he once saw from a distance a poor sinner being led to the gallows.
sentences.n: “es trug sich zu, daß …” is the fixed old idiom for ‘it came to pass that’ — the tale's high storytelling register. “ein armer Sünder” is the standard old term for a condemned criminal on his way to execution — literally ‘a poor sinner,’ half pity and half distance.

sentences.t: Er sprach so vor sich hin „jetzt wiederfährt diesem sein Recht.“
sentences.l: He said so to himself “now befalls this one his due.”
sentences.i: He said quietly to himself, “Now this one is getting what he deserves.”
sentences.n: “vor sich hin sprechen” is the fixed phrase for muttering to oneself, speaking under one's breath. “wiederfährt” (also spelled widerfährt) is from “widerfahren,” to befall, to happen to someone — with dative of the person and nominative of the thing that happens: “diesem [dat.] wiederfährt sein Recht [nom.].” The hermit's one sentence is the sin that undoes him.

sentences.t: Abends, als er das Wasser den Berg hinauftrug, erschien der Engel nicht, der ihn sonst begleitete und brachte ihm auch nicht seine Speise.
sentences.l: In the evening, as he carried the water up the mountain, the angel did not appear, who otherwise accompanied him, and did not bring him his food either.
sentences.i: In the evening, as he was carrying the water up the mountain, the angel who otherwise went with him did not appear, and did not bring him his food either.
sentences.n: “hinauftrug” is the separable “hinauftragen” (hinauf- ‘up thither’ + tragen ‘to carry’) with the particle absorbed in the subordinate clause. “sonst” here is not ‘otherwise’ in the logical sense but ‘usually, on all the other days’ — habitual sonst.

sentences.t: Da erschrack er, prüfte sein Herz und bedachte womit er wohl könnte gesündigt haben, weil Gott also zürne, aber er wußte es nicht.
sentences.l: Then he took fright, examined his heart and considered wherewith he might have sinned, since God so was angry, but he did not know it.
sentences.i: At that he took fright, searched his heart, and pondered what he might have sinned in, for God was so angry — but he could not tell.
sentences.n: “erschrack” is the 1857 spelling of “erschrak.” “prüfte sein Herz” is the plain devotional phrase — to examine one's conscience. “zürne” is the present subjunctive of “zürnen,” to be angry (with someone, dat.); the subjunctive marks the whole clause as reported thought rather than the narrator's assertion — this is what the hermit is thinking. “also” here is the old ‘so, in this way,’ not modern German “also” = ‘therefore.’

sentences.t: Da aß und trank er nicht, warf sich nieder auf die Erde und betete Tag und Nacht.
sentences.l: Then he ate and drank not, threw himself down on the earth and prayed day and night.
sentences.i: Then he neither ate nor drank, cast himself down on the ground, and prayed day and night.
sentences.n: “aß und trank er nicht” — verb-second, with the two verbs sharing the single negation and the single subject that follows. “sich niederwerfen” is the reflexive separable verb for throwing oneself down, prostrating oneself; the particle “nieder” goes down the clause.

sentences.t: Und als er einmal in dem Walde so recht bitterlich weinte, hörte er ein Vöglein, das sang so schön und herrlich, da ward er noch betrübter und sprach „wie singst du so fröhlich!
sentences.l: And when he once wept in the forest so really bitterly, he heard a little bird, which sang so beautifully and gloriously, then he grew still more sorrowful and said “how you sing so joyfully!
sentences.i: And once, as he was weeping in the forest quite bitterly, he heard a little bird that sang so sweetly and gloriously; at that he grew even sadder and said, “How joyfully you sing!
sentences.n: “betrübter” is the comparative of the adjective “betrübt,” sorrowful, downcast — “noch betrübter” = still more sorrowful. “so recht” is the intensifier ‘quite, really’ that stacks with the adverb it modifies. The bird's beauty is not comfort — it makes the grief sharper.

sentences.t: dir zürnt der Herr nicht: ach, wenn du mir sagen könntest womit ich ihn beleidigt habe, damit ich Buße thäte, und mein Herz auch wieder fröhlich würde!“
sentences.l: on you the Lord is not angry: oh, if you could tell me wherewith I have offended him, so that I might do penance, and my heart also might again become joyful!”
sentences.i: the Lord is not angry with you — ah, if you could only tell me how I have offended him, so that I might do penance and my heart might be joyful again!”
sentences.n: “Buße thun” is the fixed devotional phrase — to do penance, to make amends; “thäte” is the past subjunctive of “thun” (modern tun/täte), marking a wish. “Buße” recurs through the rest of the tale as the theme-word — penance, atonement — and always has this fixed sense: the outward act by which the inner repentance is worked out.

sentences.t: Da fieng das Vöglein an zu sprechen und sagte „du hast unrecht gethan, weil du einen armen Sünder verdammt hast, der zum Galgen geführt wurde,
sentences.l: Then the little bird began to speak and said “you have done wrong, because you condemned a poor sinner who was being led to the gallows,
sentences.i: Then the little bird began to speak and said, “You did wrong, because you condemned a poor sinner who was being led to the gallows,
sentences.n: “fieng … an” is the 1857 spelling of “fing an,” separable “anfangen,” to begin. “verdammt” is the past participle of “verdammen,” to condemn — used here in the strong religious sense: the hermit passed a judgment reserved to God.

sentences.t: darum zürnt dir der Herr; er allein hält Gericht.
sentences.l: therefore the Lord is angry with you; he alone holds judgment.
sentences.i: that is why the Lord is angry with you; he alone holds judgment.
sentences.n: “zürnt dir” — “zürnen” takes the dative of the person one is angry with: “dir zürnt der Herr” = the Lord is angry with you. “Gericht halten” is the fixed phrase, to hold court, to sit in judgment; the whole clause is the ground of the tale's teaching.

sentences.t: Doch wenn du Buße thun und deine Sünde bereuen willst, so wird er dir verzeihen.“
sentences.l: Yet if you will do penance and repent your sin, so he will forgive you.”
sentences.i: Yet if you will do penance and repent your sin, he will forgive you.”
sentences.n: “bereuen” is to repent, to feel remorse for — takes the accusative of the thing repented (“deine Sünde bereuen”). “verzeihen” takes the dative of the person forgiven — “er wird dir verzeihen,” he will forgive you. The bird's offer is stated as a plain conditional.

sentences.t: Da stand der Engel neben ihm und hatte einen trockenen Ast in der Hand und sprach „diesen trockenen Ast sollst du so lange tragen, bis drei grüne Zweige aus ihm hervorsprießen,
sentences.l: Then the angel stood beside him and had a dry branch in his hand and said “this dry branch you shall carry so long, until three green twigs sprout forth out of it,
sentences.i: Then the angel stood beside him with a dry branch in his hand and said, “This dry branch you shall carry until three green shoots sprout from it,
sentences.n: “hervorsprießen” is the separable “hervor-” (out, forth) + “sprießen” (to sprout) — to sprout forth, to burst into leaf; kept as one word here because it stays inside the “bis”-clause. “Zweige” is the plural of “der Zweig,” twig, small branch (distinct from the larger “Ast” the angel is handing him).

sentences.t: aber Nachts, wenn du schlafen willst, sollst du ihn unter dein Haupt legen.
sentences.l: but at nights, when you want to sleep, you shall lay it under your head.
sentences.i: but at night, when you would sleep, you are to lay it under your head.
sentences.n: “Nachts” is an old genitive of time, ‘by night, at night’ — the “-s” is the fossil ending, not a plural. “Haupt” is the elevated word for head (Kopf being the plain one) — the register the whole speech is pitched in.

sentences.t: Dein Brot sollst du dir an den Thüren erbitten und in demselben Hause nicht länger als eine Nacht verweilen.
sentences.l: Your bread you shall beg yourself at the doors and in the same house not longer than one night stay.
sentences.i: You shall beg your bread at people's doors, and stay no longer than a single night in any one house.
sentences.n: “Thüren” is the 1857 spelling of “Türen,” doors. “erbitten” is to ask for, to beg for (something) — with the dative reflexive (“dir erbitten”) it is to beg it for oneself. “demselben” = “dem selben,” the same. Two hard rules stated flat: beg door to door, and move on each morning.

sentences.t: Das ist die Buße, die dir der Herr auflegt.“
sentences.l: That is the penance which the Lord lays upon you.”
sentences.i: That is the penance the Lord lays upon you.”
sentences.n: “auflegen” is the separable “auf-” (on, upon) + “legen” (to lay) — to lay upon; classic in this religious use, “eine Buße auflegen,” to impose a penance. The dative “dir” is the person on whom it is laid.

sentences.t: Da nahm der Einsiedler das Stück Holz und gieng in die Welt zurück, die er so lange nicht gesehen hatte.
sentences.l: Then the hermit took the piece of wood and went back into the world, which he had not seen for so long.
sentences.i: Then the hermit took the piece of wood and went back into the world, which he had not seen in so long.
sentences.n: “zurückgehen” is separable — “gieng … zurück,” went back — the particle to the end. “so lange nicht” = for so long not — the negation and the time-word stay together in German where English separates them.

sentences.t: Er aß und trank nichts, als was man ihm an den Thüren reichte;
sentences.l: He ate and drank nothing, except what one handed to him at the doors;
sentences.i: He ate and drank nothing except what was handed to him at people's doors;
sentences.n: “als was” is the older combination for ‘except what, other than what’; a modern text would more likely say “außer was.” The impersonal “man … reichte” — literally ‘one handed’ — becomes an English passive.

sentences.t: manche Bitte aber ward nicht gehört, und manche Thüre blieb ihm verschlossen, also daß er oft ganze Tage lang keinen Krumen Brot bekam.
sentences.l: many a request however was not heard, and many a door remained closed to him, so that he often for whole days long got no crumb of bread.
sentences.i: but many a request went unheard, and many a door stayed shut to him, so that he often went whole days without a crumb of bread.
sentences.n: “ward” is the archaic past of “werden” (modern “wurde”). “also daß” is the older ‘so that,’ where modern German has “so daß / so dass.” “Krumen” is a masculine variant of the crumb-word (der Krume/Krumen, beside die Krume) — “keinen Krumen Brot” = not a crumb of bread.

sentences.t: Einmal war er vom Morgen bis Abend von Thüre zu Thüre gegangen, niemand hatte ihm etwas gegeben, niemand wollte ihn die Nacht beherbergen,
sentences.l: Once he had gone from morning until evening from door to door, nobody had given him anything, nobody wanted to lodge him for the night,
sentences.i: Once he had gone from morning till evening from door to door; no one had given him anything, no one would take him in for the night,
sentences.n: Three parallel clauses without conjunctions — the tale's plain way of piling the day's refusals on top of each other. “ihn die Nacht beherbergen” — “die Nacht” is the accusative of time, ‘for the night.’

sentences.t: da gieng er hinaus in einen Wald, und fand endlich eine angebaute Höhle, und eine alte Frau saß darin.
sentences.l: then he went out into a forest, and at last found a built-up cave, and an old woman was sitting in it.
sentences.i: so he went out into a forest, and at last found a cave built up as a dwelling, and an old woman sat within.
sentences.n: “angebaute” is the past participle of “anbauen” used adjectivally — the verb has two senses (to cultivate, of ground; to build onto, to extend a building) and here it means the cave has been built up into something habitable, a dwelling. “darin” = ‘in it,’ the “da-” prefix that stands in for a prepositional pronoun.

sentences.t: Da sprach er „gute Frau, behaltet mich diese Nacht in euerm Hause.“
sentences.l: Then he said “good woman, keep me this night in your house.”
sentences.i: Then he said, “Good woman, keep me this night in your house.”
sentences.n: “behaltet” is the plural/polite imperative of “behalten,” to keep — the old ‘ihr’-form of address to a stranger, softer than “du.” “euerm” is the 1857 spelling of “eurem” (dative of “euer,” your), the plural/polite possessive that goes with it.

sentences.t: Aber sie antwortete „nein, ich darf nicht, wenn ich auch wollte.
sentences.l: But she answered “no, I dare not, even if I wanted to.
sentences.i: But she answered, “No, I daren't, even if I wanted to.
sentences.n: “wenn ich auch wollte” — “auch” here is the concessive ‘even’; the fixed pattern is “wenn … auch …” = ‘even if…’ Her refusal is stated first; the reason comes in the next unit.

sentences.t: Ich habe drei Söhne, die sind bös und wild, wenn sie von ihrem Raubzug heim kommen und finden euch, so würden sie uns beide umbringen.“
sentences.l: I have three sons, they are wicked and wild, when they come home from their raid and find you, they would kill both of us.”
sentences.i: I have three sons, wicked and wild — when they come home from their raid and find you, they would kill the two of us.”
sentences.n: “Raubzug” is a raid, a plundering expedition (Raub- ‘plunder’ + Zug ‘expedition, campaign’); it establishes at a stroke what her sons do for a living. The sequence “wenn … so würden …” slips from present indicative to conditional as she thinks the scene through.

sentences.t: Da sprach der Einsiedler „laßt mich nur bleiben, sie werden euch und mir nichts thun,“
sentences.l: Then the hermit said “just let me stay, they will do nothing to you and to me,”
sentences.i: Then the hermit said, “Only let me stay — they will do you and me no harm,”
sentences.n: “laßt” is the 1857 spelling of “lasst,” the plural/polite imperative of “lassen,” to let. “nur” here is the softening ‘just, only.’ “nichts thun” — “thun” is the 1857 spelling of “tun”; “jemandem nichts thun” is the fixed phrase for ‘to do someone no harm.’

sentences.t: und die Frau war mitleidig und ließ sich bewegen.
sentences.l: and the woman was compassionate and let herself be moved.
sentences.i: and the woman was compassionate, and let herself be persuaded.
sentences.n: “sich bewegen lassen” is the fixed idiom for ‘to be prevailed upon, to be swayed’ — literally ‘to let oneself be moved.’ The two adjectives (mitleidig — swayed) do all the character work the tale gives her.

sentences.t: Da legte sich der Mann unter die Treppe und das Stück Holz unter seinen Kopf.
sentences.l: Then the man laid himself down under the staircase and the piece of wood under his head.
sentences.i: Then the man lay down under the staircase and put the piece of wood under his head.
sentences.n: One reflexive verb (“legte sich”) governs both prepositional phrases in parallel — the German coordinates “sich” and “das Stück Holz” under a single verb; English has to supply “and put” for the second object.

sentences.t: Wie die Alte das sah, fragte sie nach der Ursache, da erzählte er ihr daß er es zur Buße mit sich herum trage und Nachts zu einem Kissen brauche.
sentences.l: As the old woman saw that, she asked after the cause, then he told her that he was carrying it about with himself as penance and at nights needed it for a pillow.
sentences.i: When the old woman saw this, she asked the reason, and he told her that he carried it about with him as penance, and used it at night for a pillow.
sentences.n: Reported speech — the subordinate clauses (“trage … brauche”) are in the present subjunctive, marking that this is what he said, not what the narrator affirms. “zur Buße” = as penance, by way of penance.

sentences.t: Er habe den Herrn beleidigt, denn als er einen armen Sünder auf dem Gang nach dem Gericht gesehen, habe er gesagt diesem widerfahre sein Recht.
sentences.l: He had offended the Lord, for when he had seen a poor sinner on the walk to the judgment, he had said this one's due was befalling him.
sentences.i: He had offended the Lord, he said, for when he had seen a poor sinner on the way to execution, he had said that this one was getting what he deserved.
sentences.n: The reported speech continues: “habe … beleidigt,” “habe … gesagt,” “widerfahre” all subjunctive — the whole paragraph is his voice inside her hearing. “der Gang nach dem Gericht” — literally ‘the walk to the judgment/court,’ the standard phrase for the walk of the condemned to the place of execution.

sentences.t: Da fieng die Frau an zu weinen und rief „ach, wenn der Herr ein einziges Wort also bestraft, wie wird es meinen Söhnen ergehen, wenn sie vor ihm im Gericht erscheinen.“
sentences.l: Then the woman began to weep and cried “oh, if the Lord so punishes a single word, how will it fare with my sons, when they appear before him in judgment.”
sentences.i: Then the woman began to weep and cried, “Oh, if the Lord punishes a single word so, how will my sons fare when they appear before him in judgment?”
sentences.n: “wie wird es … ergehen” is the fixed idiom “jemandem ergehen,” to fare with someone — how will it go for my sons. The 1857 text ends this cry with a full stop rather than a question mark; the exclamation is left to the reader's ear.

sentences.t: Um Mitternacht kamen die Räuber heim, lärmten und tobten.
sentences.l: At midnight the robbers came home, made a din and raged.
sentences.i: At midnight the robbers came home, roaring and raging.
sentences.n: Three past-tense verbs in a row — the plain foregrounding the tale uses for their entrance. “Um Mitternacht” — “um” for a point of time on the clock, ‘at.’

sentences.t: Sie zündeten ein Feuer an, und als das die Höhle erleuchtete und sie einen Mann unter der Treppe liegen sahen, geriethen sie in Zorn und schrien ihre Mutter an,
sentences.l: They lit a fire, and when that lit up the cave and they saw a man lying under the staircase, they got into a rage and shouted at their mother,
sentences.i: They lit a fire, and when that lit up the cave and they saw a man lying under the staircase, they flew into a rage and shouted at their mother,
sentences.n: “erleuchtete” is the past of “erleuchten,” to light up, illumine; here in the plain physical sense. “geriethen” is the 1857 spelling of “gerieten,” past of “geraten” — with “in Zorn geraten” = to fly into a rage. “schrien … an” is separable “anschreien,” to shout at.

sentences.t: „wer ist der Mann? haben wirs nicht verboten irgend jemand aufzunehmen?“
sentences.l: “who is the man? have we not forbidden it to take in anyone at all?”
sentences.i: “Who is that man? Haven't we forbidden taking anyone in at all?”
sentences.n: “wirs” is “wir es,” the enclitic dropping the vowel of “es.” “aufnehmen” is separable — “aufzunehmen” is the zu-infinitive, with “zu” slotting between the particle and the stem. “irgend jemand” = anyone at all.

sentences.t: Da sprach die Mutter „laßt ihn, es ist ein armer Sünder der seine Schuld büßt.“
sentences.l: Then the mother said “let him be, it is a poor sinner who is atoning for his guilt.”
sentences.i: Then the mother said, “Let him be — it is a poor sinner who is atoning for his guilt.”
sentences.n: “büßt” is 3rd sg. present of “büßen,” to atone for, to do penance for — the verb behind “Buße.” “die Schuld büßen” is the fixed phrase for making atonement for one's guilt. Her defense is exactly the vocabulary the angel gave the hermit.

sentences.t: Die Räuber fragten „was hat er gethan?“
sentences.l: The robbers asked “what has he done?”
sentences.i: The robbers asked, “What has he done?”
sentences.n: “gethan” is the 1857 spelling of “getan” (past participle of thun/tun). One line, one question — the plain rhythm the whole scene is built on.

sentences.t: „Alter,“ riefen sie, „erzähl uns deine Sünden.“
sentences.l: “Old man,” they called, “tell us your sins.”
sentences.n: “Alter” as a bare vocative is a plain, unadorned address to an old man — nothing tender in it. The imperative singular “erzähl” (rather than plural/polite) matches the roughness of the address.

sentences.t: Der Alte erhob sich und sagte ihnen wie er mit einem einzigen Wort schon so gesündigt habe, daß Gott ihm zürne, und er für diese Schuld jetzt büße.
sentences.l: The old man raised himself and told them how he had already sinned with a single word so much, that God was angry with him, and he was now atoning for this guilt.
sentences.i: The old man raised himself up and told them how, with a single word, he had already sinned so gravely that God was angry with him, and how he was now atoning for this guilt.
sentences.n: Reported speech throughout: “gesündigt habe,” “zürne,” “büße” — three subjunctives that mark this whole span as the hermit's telling. “ihm zürne” — dative again with “zürnen.” The tale is now stating the pattern for the fourth time (the hermit's judgment, the bird's, the mother's, the hermit's own confession); the fourth time is the one that lands.

sentences.t: Den Räubern ward von seiner Erzählung das Herz so gewaltig gerührt, daß sie über ihr bisheriges Leben erschraken, in sich giengen und mit herzlicher Reue ihre Buße begannen.
sentences.l: To the robbers the heart was so mightily moved by his tale, that they took fright over their former life, went into themselves and with heartfelt remorse began their penance.
sentences.i: At his tale the robbers' hearts were so mightily moved that they took fright at their former life, went into themselves, and began their penance with heartfelt remorse.
sentences.n: “ward … das Herz … gerührt” is the dative of possession (“den Räubern”) with a passive — literally ‘the heart was moved to the robbers.’ “in sich gehen” is the fixed phrase for going into oneself, examining oneself in penitence. “bisheriges” = up to now, hitherto (bis + her + -ig-): the life they have led up until this moment. “herzlicher” is the strong dative feminine singular of “herzlich,” heartfelt.

sentences.t: Der Einsiedler, nachdem er die drei Sünder bekehrt hatte, legte sich wieder zum Schlafe unter die Treppe.
sentences.l: The hermit, after he had converted the three sinners, laid himself down again for sleep under the staircase.
sentences.i: The hermit, having converted the three sinners, lay down again to sleep under the staircase.
sentences.n: “bekehrt” is the past participle of “bekehren,” to convert (someone to a faith or a right way) — the strong religious verb. “zum Schlafe” — dative with the fossil “-e,” “for sleep, to sleep,” the older ending on masculine/neuter datives that 1857 still writes on some fixed phrases.

sentences.t: Am Morgen aber fand man ihn todt, und aus dem trocknen Holz, auf welchem sein Haupt lag, waren drei grüne Zweige hoch empor gewachsen.
sentences.l: In the morning however he was found dead, and out of the dry wood, on which his head lay, three green twigs had grown high aloft.
sentences.i: But in the morning he was found dead, and out of the dry wood on which his head rested, three green twigs had grown high up.
sentences.n: “empor” is the old adverb for ‘up, aloft, upward’ — “hoch empor gewachsen” = grown high up. “trocknen” here is the strong dative singular of the adjective “trocken” (dry), syncopated — not a form of the verb “trocknen” (to dry). “Haupt” again the elevated word for head, echoing the angel's speech at the outset.

sentences.t: Also hatte ihn der Herr wieder in Gnaden zu sich aufgenommen.
sentences.l: Thus had the Lord taken him back to himself in mercy.
sentences.i: So the Lord had taken him back to himself in mercy.
sentences.n: “also” is the older ‘so, in this way, thus’ — not modern “also” = ‘therefore.’ “in Gnaden aufnehmen” is the fixed phrase, ‘to receive graciously, to take back into favor’; the perfect (“hatte … aufgenommen”) closes the tale looking back on what has already been done.

glossary.behaltet: behalten — keep (imperative pl./polite; „behaltet mich“ = keep me, lodge me)
glossary.bitte: die Bitte — request, plea (fem. noun; „manche Bitte ward nicht gehört“ = many a request went unheard)
glossary.ergehen: ergehen — to fare, to go (impers. with dat.; „wie wird es meinen Söhnen ergehen“ = how will it go for my sons)
glossary.erquickt: erquicken — refreshed, revived (past part.; „manche Pflanze damit erquickt“ = many a plant refreshed by it)
glossary.essen: das Essen — food, meal (neuter noun; substantival infinitive; „brachte ihm sein Essen“ = brought him his food)
glossary.kreißen: kreißen — to wheel, to circle (in flight) (older verb beside kreisen; not the modern kreißen ‘to be in labor’)
glossary.trocknen: trocken — dry (strong dat. sg. of the adjective, syncopated; „aus dem trocknen Holz“ = out of the dry wood; not a form of the verb trocknen)
